query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled atmospheric plasma oxidation treatment applied to boride-based components will form an ultra-thin, dense, self-healing oxide barrier that significantly improves resistance to molten aluminum corrosion compared to untreated components.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components currently exhibiting microstructures that allow molten aluminum infiltration during hot-dip aluminum-plating.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled atmospheric plasma oxidation treatment at approximately 700°C for a precisely tuned exposure time.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at 660–700°C under hot-dip aluminum-plating process conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-thin, adherent oxide (or mixed oxide-boride) barrier on the component surface.
generation.mechanism: The plasma treatment promotes rapid oxidation at the surface that produces a compact and self-healing oxide layer, which acts as a barrier to limit aluminum diffusion and chemical attack during exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated components will demonstrate a measurably lower rate of corrosion and reduced depth of aluminum infiltration relative to untreated boride-based samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated boride-based components under identical molten aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to hold under standard hot-dip conditions (660–700°C) but may be compromised if the oxide layer is mechanically abraded or if treatment parameters fall outside the optimized range.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal plasma oxidation parameters (e.g., exact temperature and duration) required to consistently produce an effective oxide barrier that maintains long-term stability under cyclic thermal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based samples: one set receiving the controlled atmospheric plasma oxidation treatment and one untreated set. Subject both sets to prolonged immersion in molten aluminum at 660–700°C. Evaluate and compare the corrosion performance.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via microscopy and spectroscopy)
Aluminum infiltration depth (using cross-sectional elemental mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance metrics (lower corrosion rate and reduced aluminum infiltration) compared to the untreated controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

frame.system: Boride-based components currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment
frame.limitation: The components are vulnerable to attack by molten aluminum due to their current surface state/microstructure, which does not effectively prevent aluminum infiltration or chemical attack.
constraints: A single intervention must be identified
The intervention should provide a measurable improvement relative to a baseline (untreated or standard material)
The hypothesis must include a mechanism, defined operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment for falsification
frame.regime: High-temperature exposure to molten aluminum (typically around 660–700°C), representative of the plating process conditions
prior_attempts: Conventional alloy modifications or coatings have been attempted but may have fallen short due to poor adhesion or instability in the molten aluminum environment
Other surface treatments might have been used without engineering a self-limiting barrier layer, leading to insufficient corrosion mitigation

decision.trend: Earlier studies on corrosion‐resistant metallic systems have increasingly turned to surface modification rather than bulk alloying. For instance, PMC7240591 demonstrated that an atmospheric-pressure plasma jet (APPJ) treatment creates a thin, oxidized surface layer on a medium-entropy alloy to improve corrosion resistance, while later work such as PMC10221107 employed boronizing to form surface boride layers that enhance hardness and wear but do not directly address molten-metal infiltration. These studies show a progression from simply altering bulk composition to actively engineering the surface/interface to form protective layers. Nonetheless, in many cases the self-limiting nature and adhesion of such barriers have been insufficient when facing aggressive environments like molten aluminum.
decision.unsolved: The key challenge remaining is to design a robust, self-healing interfacial barrier on boride-based components that can withstand prolonged exposure to molten aluminum (~660–700°C), effectively blocking aluminum infiltration and chemical attack without the adhesion and stability issues seen in previous coatings or alloy modifications.
decision.lever: Develop a controlled plasma oxidation treatment that creates an ultra-thin, dense, self-healing oxide barrier on the boride component surface. Key parameters would involve tuning the plasma temperature (around 700°C) and exposure time to form an optimized, adherent oxide (or mixed oxide-boride) layer that prevents aluminum diffusion.
decision.why: This approach logically follows the trend of using plasma-based surface treatments (as demonstrated in PMC7240591) to modify interface chemistry and has the potential to yield a self-limiting barrier. By focusing on a surface engineering strategy rather than bulk alloy composition changes, it directly targets the issues of molten aluminum attack on boride-based components identified in the current limitations and past attempts.
